text: The Hall family owned land and were clothiers. They ran the whole business of making cloth, from sheep farmers and shearers to weavers, fullers and buyers. Around 1610 John Hall and his wife Elizabeth built The Hall on medieval foundations, facing a river that powered the family's fulling mills and, later, its looms.
source_title: Who Were The Halls?
source_author: The Hall / Alex Moulton Charitable Trust (no named author)
uncertainty: The page gives no author or date; the year comes from the URL path. Historic England's listing names the builder as John Hall II, c.1610. The page says the family's landholding may go back to 1170, and marks this only as possible.

text: Historic England's garden listing says that when John Hall II died in 1631 the house went to Rachel Baynton. She married into the Pierrepoint family, later Dukes of Kingston, and the house was renamed Kingston House. By the late 1700s the owners seldom lived there and it served as a farmhouse.
source_title: The Hall, Bradford-on-Avon (Register of Parks and Gardens, list entry 1001233)
source_author: Historic England
uncertainty: The listing text was written in 2000 and edited up to 2004. It conflicts with the Moulton Trust page 'Who Were The Halls?', which says the last Hall to live there, John Hall the younger, died in 1710 and left the house to his illegitimate daughter Rachel Baynton. Historic England gives Rachel's death as 1722.

text: In 1805 Thomas Divett, a City of London man, bought the estate. He replaced an old corn mill southwest of the house with a cloth mill and used the house itself as a wool store. The mill later failed in a slump in the town's cloth trade, and the house and land were put up for sale in 1848.
source_title: The Hall, Bradford-on-Avon (Register of Parks and Gardens, list entry 1001233)
source_author: Historic England
uncertainty: The VCH Wiltshire vol. 7 (1953) dates Divett's purchase to 1802. VCH vol. 4 (1959) says the five-storey Kingston mill was built in 1811 and stood idle from 1842. Grace's Guide spells the name 'Divitt' and says only 'early 19th century'.

text: Bradford's clothmaking shrank fast after about 1815. There were about 19 manufacturers in 1820, 14 in 1826 and only 5 by 1833. The town kept to broadcloth while export demand for it fell, and by 1838 it had just four mills employing 418 people.
source_title: Textile industries since 1550, in A History of the County of Wiltshire: Volume 4 (British History Online)
source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
uncertainty: The Moulton Trust's woollen-trade page gives 32 factories in 1800 and 5 in 1838, against the VCH figure of four mills in 1838. The two sources may be counting different things.

text: In the early 1840s fashion moved towards bright, lightweight, intricately woven fabrics, and demand for the town's traditional cloth fell. Then in 1841 the local bank failed. It had invested heavily in two of the largest mills. More than 400 workers were hit, the workhouse could not cope, and many people left to find work.
source_title: What Happened To The Woollen Trade?
source_author: The Hall / Alex Moulton Charitable Trust (no named author)
uncertainty: The year comes from the URL path. VCH vol. 4 names the bank as Hobhouse & Co., which failed in autumn 1841, and the two failed firms as Coopers of Staverton and Saunders of Bradford. The Preservation Trust calls it the Hobhouse, Phillott & Lowder bank in Church Street.

text: In 1791 about 500 cloth workers gathered at Westbury House, the home of clothier Joseph Phelps, to protest against a new scribbling machine. Shots fired from the house killed three people, one of them a child. The crowd then burned the machine on the town bridge. The coroner ruled the killings justifiable and awarded Phelps £250.
source_title: Poverty and protest: the dark side of the industry that enriched Bradford (review of Rosie MacGregor, Remnants and Yarns)
source_author: Andrew Eberlin, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
uncertainty: The casualty figures differ between sources. This review says three dead including a child. The Moulton Trust says a man, a woman and a child. The Tolpuddle Martyrs Museum says one man killed and two mortally wounded. VCH vol. 4 calls it a carding machine adapted for scribbling. The Moulton Trust gives the date as 14 May 1791. The review shows '17 Feb' with no year.

text: There were disputes over pay before the machine riots. The town's first recorded riot, in November 1726, was against more work for less pay. In 1787 weavers rioted over wages. The clothiers reportedly promised not to build bigger loom shops if the weavers accepted lower rates.
source_title: Poverty and protest: the dark side of the industry that enriched Bradford (review of Rosie MacGregor, Remnants and Yarns)
source_author: Andrew Eberlin, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
uncertainty: The 1787 promise is reported second-hand ('reportedly'). VCH vol. 4 also records riots in 1726 across Bradford, Trowbridge, Melksham and Frome.

text: In 1803 women made up about two-fifths of the weavers in Bradford and Trowbridge. Across the county that year, weavers might work 13 to 17 hours a day for roughly 7s 6d to 10s a week.
source_title: Textile industries since 1550, in A History of the County of Wiltshire: Volume 4 (British History Online)
source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
uncertainty: The hours and wages are figures for the whole county, not for Bradford alone.

text: Numbers 1 to 18 Middle Rank are a terrace of weavers' houses built in the late 1600s. Most are two storeys with attic rooms in the gables and stone-mullioned casement windows. Part of the row has since been rebuilt. The terrace was listed Grade II in 1963 for its value to the townscape.
source_title: 1-18 Middle Rank, Bradford-on-Avon (listed building entry)
source_author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
uncertainty: The entry was amended in 1974. The rebuilding of nos. 5-18 is described only as 'recent' relative to the listing text.

text: Stephen Moulton was Charles Goodyear's agent. He brought the first samples of vulcanised rubber to Britain and shared them with Thomas Hancock, who won the British vulcanisation patent in 1843, a few weeks ahead of Goodyear. Disputes over patents and rights followed, and in 1848 Moulton started his own firm at Kingston Mill.
source_title: S. Moulton and Co
source_author: Grace's Guide to British Industrial History (wiki, no named author)
uncertainty: The page does not say how Hancock used the samples. VCH vol. 4 (1959) adds that Moulton had his own 1847 patent, which offered an alternative to both the Goodyear and Hancock processes. Wikipedia repeats the sample story, citing Grace's Guide and a commercial site.

text: Moulton's start-up depended on American partners and skills. He made an 1847 agreement with the Rider brothers and James Thomas of New York. In 1848 an American engineer, Mr Frost, oversaw the machinery, and an American foreman and forewoman, S. P. Abbot and Amelia Fisher, followed him. Woollen workers who had lost their jobs supplied the local labour.
source_title: Other industries, in A History of the County of Wiltshire: Volume 4 (British History Online)
source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
uncertainty: The VCH says the Riders were partners for four years from 1850. No wage or working-condition details are given.

text: Bradford on Avon Museum says Moulton was backed by Goodyear and by his friend Septimus Palairet of Woolley. He picked the town for its empty powered mills and its workers already used to factory work. He supplied buffers, springs and hoses to Brunel's Great Western Railway, and rubber-coated cloth for army capes after the Crimean War began in 1853.
source_title: Rubber Industry
source_author: Bradford on Avon Museum
uncertainty: The page has no author or date. The Moulton Trust's woollen-trade page names the backer 'Captain Palairet of Woolley Grange'.

text: The Moulton works specialised in rubber for engineering, above all railway springs, bearings, and buffer and draw-bar springs. It also made hose, tubing, belting, washers and valves. Sales of springs and rings alone rose from about £3,600 in 1857 to nearly £58,000 by 1890.
source_title: Other industries, in A History of the County of Wiltshire: Volume 4 (British History Online)
source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
uncertainty: The exact figures are £3,572 (1857) and £57,720 (1890). The Moulton Trust claims Spencer Moulton later supplied rubber parts to 80% of the world's railway companies; this is unverified and promotional.

text: The Moulton firm's workforce started small and grew slowly: 78 people in 1850, only 52 in 1875, 164 by 1900 and 793 by 1950.
source_title: Other industries, in A History of the County of Wiltshire: Volume 4 (British History Online)
source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
uncertainty: Moulton Trust pages say almost everyone in the town worked at the factory over nearly 150 years. Against these figures, that claim is a generalisation and may fit the 20th century better.

text: The 'Iron Duke' calender, named after Wellington, was designed in America and built in Britain in 1849 for Kingston Mill. It pressed rubber onto woven cloth to make waterproof sheeting. When Avon demolished the mill in 1972, the machine went to Bristol's new Industrial Museum. It was put back on show at the site in 2016.
source_title: UK puts 19th century rubber calender on display
source_author: European Rubber Journal (no named author)
uncertainty: Grace's Guide dates the machine c.1848 and its removal to 1973. Dorothea Restorations also says it was stored at M Shed from 1973. The unveiling is given as September 2016 (Dorothea Restorations) and November 2016 (Grace's Guide). bradfordonavon.co.uk calls it the first machine of its type in Europe.

text: George Spencer was testing rubber for railway springs and shock absorbers. He judged Moulton's product the best for the purpose and set up his own firm in the early 1850s. In 1891 the two businesses merged as George Spencer, Moulton and Co.
source_title: George Spencer, Moulton and Co
source_author: Grace's Guide to British Industrial History (wiki, no named author)
uncertainty: VCH vol. 4 dates Spencer's London firm to 1853 and says it took over direction of the business at the 1891 merger.

text: New Mills, now part of the Kingston Mills group, was built as a woollen mill by James Harper and Thomas Taylor, with 1869 carved on its pediment. Cloth-making there stopped in 1898. Soon afterwards Spencer, Moulton and Co took over the empty buildings and converted them for rubber around 1900. Rubber was made there until 1992.
source_title: New Mills (Buildings 72-75), Kingston Mills, Bradford-on-Avon (listed building entry)
source_author: Historic England (via British Listed Buildings)
uncertainty: The neighbouring rubber-store listing says Spencer Moulton bought New Mills in 1899. The 2012 town trail says rubber production at New Mill continued under Avon until 1994, which conflicts with the listing's 1992.

text: Abbey Mill on Church Street was built as a cloth mill by Richard Gane for Harper, Taylor and Co, and stopped making cloth in 1898. It was later used mainly by the rubber firms Spencer Moulton and then Avon. After the factory closed in 1995, the building was converted into retirement apartments.
source_title: Bradford on Avon Town Trail
source_author: Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust, Bradford on Avon Museum and Tourist Information Centre
uncertainty: The dates conflict. The trail gives 1874 for the build and 1898 for the end of cloth. Archiseek and the Preservation Trust review give 1875 and 1902, and the Grade II* listing gives 1875. VCH vol. 4 says Spencer Moulton bought the Church Street and Abbey mills in 1926. Archiseek says the mill was a barracks in WWI and that Avon worked there until the early 1990s.

text: Greenland Mills housed the Sirdar Rubber Works. Sirdar went bankrupt in 1914, and in 1915 the Avon India Rubber Company took over the works and about 300 workers. Avon had started in a run-down cloth mill at Limpley Stoke and later moved to Melksham.
source_title: Avon India-Rubber Co
source_author: Grace's Guide to British Industrial History (wiki, no named author)
uncertainty: VCH vol. 4 says Sirdar was at Greenland from 1898 to 1915. The Preservation Trust review says Greenland Upper Mill made woollen cloth until 1906 and was the town's last cloth factory, while bradfordonavon.co.uk says the last mill closed in 1905. Cloth and rubber may therefore have shared the Greenland group of buildings. Grace's Spencer Moulton page says Avon's successors made tennis balls at Greenland until the late 1980s.

text: In January 1956 the Avon India Rubber Company of Melksham bought Spencer Moulton outright. The Bradford firm kept its name, and a plan that year moved Avon's general rubber goods production to the Bradford works.
source_title: Other industries, in A History of the County of Wiltshire: Volume 4 (British History Online)
source_author: Victoria County History, ed. Elizabeth Crittall
uncertainty: Grace's Guide and the Museum page give only '1956'. The Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre says Alex Moulton left the firm in 1956 to found Moulton Developments.

text: The Spencer Moulton archive at the Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre covers the firm from its founding in 1848 to the Avon takeover in 1956. It holds more than 240 volumes, including a nearly complete run of wage books from 1850 to the 1940s, over 3,600 plans, and photographs of products such as railway buffers.
source_title: Breaking the Mould: Cataloguing the archives of Spencer Moulton and Dr Alex Moulton
source_author: Tom Plant, Project Archivist, Wiltshire and Swindon History Centre
uncertainty: Cataloguing was funded by a National Archives grant in 2019; Wiltshire Council's news release gives £39,000 and about 18 months. Covid delayed the start to January 2021. No catalogue reference numbers are given.

text: Margaret Dobson's book A Vanished World recalls the Kingston Mill rubber works at the centre of town. Anyone crossing the Town Bridge passed it, and its hooters could be heard all over town. When it closed in 1992, staff were offered jobs at other company sites, but local shops and pubs lost much of their trade.
source_title: A Vanished World by Margaret Dobson (book review)
source_author: Angela and David Moss, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
uncertainty: The review is undated, and it links the book to Bradford on Avon Museum without saying exactly how. Closure dates vary across sources: 1991 (Moulton Trust, Island Site), 1992 (this review, Historic England listings, Moulton Trust 170-years page), 1993 (Grace's Guide) and 1994-1995 (town trail, Museum page). Different buildings probably closed at different times.

text: Former workers remembered constant dirt from soot and carbon black, and a separate canteen room for men covered in black powder. Some jobs, such as checking the bounce of every tennis ball, were very dull. Smoking in the workshops could get you sacked, so breaks were taken outside by the river. A Works Committee existed from 1918.
source_title: A Vanished World by Margaret Dobson (book review)
source_author: Angela and David Moss, Bradford on Avon Preservation Trust
uncertainty: The review summarises workers' recollections collected in the book, and most memories are not dated. The review also mentions the Moulton-funded Spencer Moulton Sports and Social Club, which cost six old pence a week.

text: Linden Homes Western redeveloped the former rubber factory site as Kingston Mills. The scheme, designed by Nash Partnership, has 171 converted and new homes plus shops, a café and restaurant space. In 2012 it won Best Mixed Use at the Sunday Times British Homes Awards.
source_title: Linden Homes wins Sunday Times award for historic riverside development in Bradford-on-Avon
source_author: Linden Homes
uncertainty: This is the developer's own release. Engain's ecology page says planning consent took 15 years and records lesser horseshoe and brown long-eared bat colonies on site. The Moulton Trust says Avon left the Island Site factory in 1991 and it was demolished in 2011.
